newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ten SAfrica policemen seek pardon for 1988 killing.
newsitem.headline: Ten SAfrica policemen seek pardon for 1988 killing.

text.p: Former South African police commissioner Johan van der Merwe and nine other officers have asked for amnesty for the death of an imprisoned black activist in 1988, the truth commission said on Thursday.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, headed by Nobel Peace Laureate Desmond Tutu, said in a statement the officers had applied for amnesty for a range of crimes arising from the death of Stanza Bopape in a Johannesburg police prison in 1988.
Van der Merwe was head of the police security branch at the time.

"The police claimed at the time that Bopape escaped from custody. Now 10 security policemen have made applications for amnesty in respect of a range of charges arising from his killing," the commission said.
It said five of the officers acknowledged in their amnesty applications that Bopape, an activist of the anti-apartheid United Democratic Front, had died while being interrogated.
South African radio reports that the Bopape family will oppose the amnesty applications because they doubt that a full public disclosure has been made.
"The amnesty applicants say Bopape was tied to a chair for the administration of the (electric) shocks, and alleged that he slumped forward after only two or three shocks were administered.

"In their application they say the shocks administered should not have been fatal and that they suspected he suffered from a possible heart ailment," the commission said, adding that Bopape's killing had been shrouded in a cloud of cover-ups.

It said ex-police minister Adriaan Vlok told parliament in April 1989 that Bopape had escaped while pointing out "certain spots in connection with the acts of terror in which he was allegedly involved".
Vlok also said at the time that police had witnesses who would testify that they had seen Bopape after his escape.
Bopape's body was allegedly dumped near the Komati River in the northeastern Mpumalanga province. His remains have never been found.
The truth body said the officers would testify shortly before an amnesty committee.

The committee, set up by President Nelson Mandela to help heal the wounds of the past, has the power to pardon human rights abusers on full disclosure of all relevant facts regarding their apartheid crimes.
